shippingNews.postTitle: USCG Buoy Tender Sequoia Towed Back to Port Huron

stories.body: USCG Sequoia under tow of Erica Kobasic and Nickelena. [Rosann Hollinger] STURGEON BAY, WI – The USCG buoy tender Sequoia has been at Bay Shipbuilding Co. in Sturgeon Bay, WI, for gearbox repairs the past several months, but Monday she was headed back to her Port Huron, MI, home port under tow. The tug Nickelena was on the bow and Erika Kobasic was at the stern. A new gearbox is being made and Sequoia will return to the yard in the spring to have it installed. todayInHistory.title: Sam Laud
todayInHistory.text: Sam Laud Bay Shipbuilding Corp. of Sturgeon Bay, WI, laid the keel for their hull # 712 on Jan. 4, 1974 to be built as a smaller-sized Great Lakes self-unloading bulk cargo carrier. The new vessel was launched on Nov. 19, 1974 for Buffalo's American Steamship Co. (ASC), a subsidiary of GATX Corp., Chicago, IL. Completed in 1975, the self-unloader was christened Sam Laud by Mrs. Edna Laud on behalf of her husband at a christening ceremony held April 15, 1975. Mr. Laud was the former president (1945) and chairman of the board (1956) of GATX Corp., having started with the company in 1916 as shop painter and riveter. Mr. Laud died August 1, 1963. GATX Corp. had acquired ASC in July of 1973. Mrs. Laud was accompanied by Mr. Frederick G. Jaicks, chairman and CEO of Inland Steel Co., Chicago, IL, who gave the address at the christening ceremonies. One of a new generation of self-unloaders for the ASC fleet, the Sam Laud was built at an approximate cost of $13.3 million and was the fourth of 10 self-unloaders launched for the fleet under Chapter XI of the Merchant Marine Act of 1970. Under this act, the U.S. government-guaranteed financing and tax deferred benefits for fleet modernizing. The other ASC self-unloaders built under this program were the Roger M. Kyes (now Adam E. Cornelius, 1973), Charles E. Wilson (now John J. Boland, 1973), H. Lee White (1974), St. Clair (1976), Belle River (now Walter J. marineWeather.synopsis: 30.3 inch high pressure becomes centered over northern Ontario and the Upper Great Lakes this morning. By Friday afternoon, the high builds to 30.5 inches over southern Quebec as a 29.5 inch low moves into eastern Montana. By Saturday afternoon, the high continues into New England as the low lifts north of Lake Winnipeg into northern Manitoba, strengthening to 29.2 inches by Saturday evening. The low then lifts northeast to Hudson Bay Saturday night through Sunday as it drags a 30.2 inch trough across Lake Superior. High pressure of at least 30.6 inches over the Canadian Prairies on Monday pushes ridging of at least 30.4 inches over the Upper Great Lakes early next week.

A Dense Fog Advisory is in effect until 1 PM CDT this afternoon for the northern portions of Lake Michigan. This fog may spread southward and linger into tonight and Friday morning. Fog may develop in southern portions of the lake as well tonight into Friday morning, with patchy dense fog possible. High pressure around 30.3 inches will gradually shift eastward through Friday, while strengthening to around 30.5 inches over southern Quebec. Light winds will continue through today, increasing a bit out of the south on Friday behind the strengthening high. Southerly winds will then persist through the weekend, between the high to the east and a cold front to the northwest. Winds will shift to the north and northeast behind the cold front on Monday.
High pressure, 30.40 inches, builds over the area today. This high migrates toward southern Quebec by Friday then sinks southward to New England this weekend.

High pressure 30.30 inches will slowly move south across the eastern Great Lakes through Saturday, strengthening to 30.60 inches. High pressure will continue to push south along the East Coast on Sunday and Monday, weakening to 30.30 inches.

A high pressure ridge averaging 30.4 inches continues to exit toward the Canadian Maritimes before a weak cold front sweeps southeastward across the lake through this afternoon. Behind the front, another ridge averaging 30.5 inches affects the lake through this weekend as the embedded high pressure center moves southeastward across the Great Lakes through Friday and then moves farther southeastward to Atlantic waters near Long Island and New Jersey by Sunday. This ridge should begin to exit southeastward Sunday night and a cold front should sweep southeastward across the lake on Monday.
